intro.html: Some speech is not just loud but angry, long and bitter. This topic gives you words for the kinds of angry speech, for the force behind them and for noise in general, from a crowd’s clamor to a band’s cacophony.

Angry speeches: a tirade (long and angry), a diatribe (a bitter attack), a harangue (a loud lecture). The words themselves: invective (abusive language), vitriolic (burning like acid). The force: vehement (intense), vociferous (loud about opinions), strident (harsh, grating). Noise: clamor (shouting), cacophony (clashing sounds).
Two Latin parts help: voc means voice (vociferous, vocal), and the Greek phon means sound (cacophony, telephone, symphony).

words.def: a long, angry speech, often scolding someone
words.ex: After the ball broke his window, the neighbor launched into a ten-minute {tirade} about careless children.
words.ctx: Instead of calmly explaining the problem, the manager went on a {tirade}, shouting at the staff for half an hour about every mistake made that month.
words.etym: From French tirade, “a long speech,” from Italian tirata (a pull, a volley), from tirare (to pull).

mn.cue: TIRE-ade: so long it TIRES you out
mn.text: Grandpa Gus rants about the ball in his tulips for so long that the children are worn out just listening: it is a {tirade}.

scene.alt: A grandfather rants on and on about a ball in his garden while two children grow sleepy.

words.def: a bitter, sharply critical attack in speech or writing
words.ex: His letter to the editor was a {diatribe} against the new parking rules.
words.ctx: The review was less a careful critique than a {diatribe}: page after page of bitter attacks on the director, with hardly a word about the film itself.
words.etym: From Greek diatribe, “a passing of time, a discussion,” from diatribein (to wear away): dia (through) + tribein (to rub).

mn.cue: DIA-TRIBE: words that RUB you raw
mn.text: The critic reads out his long, bitter scroll about the bakery: “Stale! Sour! Shameful!” His {diatribe} rubs poor Nell raw.

scene.alt: An angry critic reads a long, bitter attack on a bakery while the baker looks hurt.

words.def: a long, loud lecture meant to scold or stir people up
words.ex: The coach’s halftime {harangue} could be heard from the parking lot.
words.ctx: Grandpa’s {harangue} about wasting electricity went on for twenty minutes, until everyone in the house had switched off every light they could find.
words.etym: From French harangue, a speech to a crowd.

mn.cue: ha-RANG: it RANG in our ears
mn.text: Coach Ada lectures the team at the top of her lungs for twenty minutes, and her words rang in their ears all night: a real {harangue}.

labels.text: ha-RANG: it RANG in our ears

scene.alt: A fierce coach shouts a long lecture at two players, who cover their ears.

words.ex: The two rival chefs traded {invective} across the crowded kitchen.
words.ctx: The debate began politely, but it soon sank into {invective}, with both speakers calling each other names instead of discussing the question.
words.etym: From Late Latin invectivus, “abusive,” from invehi (to attack with words), literally “to carry oneself against.”

mn.text: When his kite gets stuck in a tree, Rex lets fly a swarm of stinging insults at everyone nearby: his {invective} stings like a cloud of bees.

scene.alt: An angry man shouts insults that fly like stinging bees toward a man who hides his face.

words.def: bitterly harsh and cruel in speech or writing
words.ex: The {vitriolic} review hurt the young author’s feelings for weeks.
words.ctx: The once-friendly letters between the two inventors turned {vitriolic}; each accused the other of stealing ideas and used the harshest words he could find.
words.etym: From vitriol, an old name for a burning acid, from Latin vitrum (glass), because some of its crystals look like glass.

mn.text: The angry letter is so bitter that it seems to smoke on the page, like acid eating through paper: it is {vitriolic}.

scene.alt: A woman is shocked by a letter so bitter it seems to smoke in her hands.

words.ex: Despite her {vehement} protests, Maya was given the early shift.
words.ctx: The town’s reaction to the plan was {vehement}; hundreds of residents packed the meeting hall, many shouting that they would never let the park be paved.

mn.cue: VERY-MEANT: he VERY much MEANT it
mn.text: Asked whether he broke the lamp, Theo shakes his head so hard his hat flies off: “NO!” He very much means it; his denial is {vehement}.

scene.alt: A toddler shakes his head so hard his hat flies off, shouting no, next to a fallen lamp.

words.def: loud and forceful in expressing opinions
words.ex: The {vociferous} fans cheered every single point.
words.ctx: The parents were {vociferous} in their support of the library, filling the meeting with loud speeches and signs demanding that it stay open.
words.etym: From Latin vociferari, “to shout”: vox (voice) + ferre (to carry).
words.note: Vociferous is about being loud, not about using many words; a wordy person is verbose.

mn.cue: VOC = VOICE: a VOICE that carries
mn.text: Nana Lou cheers so loudly at every game that the players can hear her from the far end of the field: she is a {vociferous} fan.

scene.alt: A grandmother shouts through a megaphone at a game while her embarrassed grandson hides his face.

words.def: loud and harsh; forceful in a grating way
words.ex: The {strident} car alarm went off at three in the morning.
words.ctx: Her tone grew {strident} as the argument went on, her voice rising to a harsh, grating pitch that made everyone at the table wince.
words.etym: From Latin stridere, “to creak, to shriek.”

mn.text: Sami saws away at his violin, and the strings shriek so harshly that the dog howls along: the sound is {strident}.

scene.alt: A boy scrapes harshly on a violin while the dog howls.

words.def: a loud, confused noise, especially of people demanding something
words.ex: The {clamor} of the crowd outside drowned out the speaker.
words.ctx: When the store announced a half-price sale, the {clamor} at its doors grew so loud that the manager opened an hour early just to quiet the shouting shoppers.
words.etym: From Latin clamor, “a shout,” from clamare (to cry out).

mn.text: At feeding time, the penguins crowd around the keeper, all squawking at once for clams and fish: what a {clamor}!

scene.alt: Three penguins squawk at once for fish while the keeper holds up his bucket.

words.def: a harsh, jarring mix of sounds
words.ex: Car horns, sirens and barking dogs made a {cacophony} outside my window.
words.ctx: Unlike the sweet harmony of the choir, the first rehearsal of the beginner band was a {cacophony}, with every player honking a different note at a different speed.

mn.text: On the first day of band practice, every beginner plays a different song at once, and Professor Edwin covers his ears: the result is a {cacophony}.

scene.alt: A beginner band plays a jumble of clashing notes while an old professor covers his ears, dizzy.

after.html: vociferous means loud, not wordy: a vociferous fan shouts, while a verbose speaker simply uses too many words. cacophony (bad sound) has a pleasant opposite, euphony (good sound), from the Greek eu, good.

after.name: vo-cloze

opts.s: The neighbors were {vociferous} in their complaints, shouting at the meeting until the plan was dropped.

after.cap: Loud and forceful about opinions: vociferous.

items.q: True or false: a vociferous speaker is one who uses far too many words.
items.why: False. Vociferous means loud and forceful (voc, voice). Using too many words is being verbose.

items.q: What is the opposite of a cacophony?
items.why: A cacophony is a clash of harsh sounds; harmony (or euphony) is sound that fits together pleasantly.

items.q: The principal spoke loudly to the whole school for thirty minutes about running in the halls. It was a…
items.why: A long, loud lecture to a group is a harangue.
Phon means sound, as in telephone and symphony; caco means bad.
